The young illusionist (who goes by 'Symmetry Silkmoth' - because why not) begins the show with her signature act, in which she somehow holds parlance with her own reflection in a large antique mirror. The two Symmetrys (who seem to move independently of one another) speak upon their morbid anxieties and intrusive thoughts - which, it transpires, form the themes of the show at large. Even though I have my theories about how the trick is achieved, to a less cynical eye it would present a thoroughly convincing spectacle.

The mysterious Miss Silkmoth rounds off her performance with a surprisingly comedic set-piece in which she attempts to communicate with her 'Departed Uncle Gregory', who appears as an apparation within a crystal ball. However, it doesn't go to plan and the audience laughs as Symmetry is put 'on hold' in her disastrous attempt to telephone the afterlife.
Overall, the show is a triumph; a brush with mysticism that stays with you long after the final bow.
